## Place mimicry-js generators directly as field values, use Faker inside arrow functions

_critical · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Put `oneOf`, `sequence`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `unique` and `withPrev` directly as a field value
or inside a static nested object. Inside an arrow function, use the Faker equivalent instead, for
example `faker.helpers.arrayElement([...])` for `oneOf`.

**Why.** mimicry-js resolves generators only where it walks the `fields` object. An arrow function's body is
opaque to it, so a generator returned from one ends up in the built object as a descriptor. The
test then compares against an object, not a string, and the failure message points nowhere near
the builder.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
fields: {
  profile: () => ({ theme: oneOf("light", "dark") }),
}
```

**Correct:**

```ts
fields: {
  theme: oneOf("light", "dark"),
  profile: () => ({ theme: faker.helpers.arrayElement(["light", "dark"]) }),
}
```

## Set every value the test asserts on explicitly when you build test data

_high · any_

**Rule.** Build test data from a builder or factory, and pass an explicit override for every field the test
asserts on or branches on. Leave random values only in fields the test never looks at. Use named
variants (traits) for whole states such as "admin" or "inactive" instead of repeating the same
overrides in many tests.

**Why.** An assertion against a randomly generated value passes or fails depending on the seed, and a
reader cannot tell from the test which value matters. An explicit override documents the input the
test depends on and makes the failure reproducible.

## Wrap function-typed fields in fixed() so the builder does not call them

_high · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** For a field whose value is itself a function (`onClick`, `onSubmit`, a formatter), wrap the
function in `fixed(fn)`. Leave a bare arrow function only where you want a fresh value on each build.

**Why.** mimicry-js calls any function it finds as a field value, so a bare callback is replaced by its return
value and the built object has `undefined` where a handler should be.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const buttonPropsBuilder = build<ButtonProps>({ fields: { label: "Save", onClick: () => {} } });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const buttonPropsBuilder = build<ButtonProps>({ fields: { label: "Save", onClick: fixed(() => {}) } });
```

## Build with .one() and .many() and pass overrides or traits for asserted values

_high · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Call `.one({ overrides })` for a single object and `.many(count, { overrides })` for a list.
Define recurring states as `traits` in the builder and apply them with `.one({ traits: "admin" })`.
The builder methods are `.one()` and `.many()`, not `.build()` or `.buildMany()`.

**Why.** Hand-written objects drift from the type, and `Array.from()` loops skip traits and overrides.
Calling methods that do not exist on a mimicry-js builder is the drift this note was written to
stop.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const user = userBuilder.build();
const users = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => userBuilder.build());
await expect(canvas.getByText(user.name)).toBeVisible();
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const user = userBuilder.one({ overrides: { name: "Ada Lovelace" } });
const admins = userBuilder.many(3, { traits: "admin" });
await expect(canvas.getByText("Ada Lovelace")).toBeVisible();
```

## Write TypeScript builders with mimicry-js and Faker

_high · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Write every TypeScript builder with `build<T>()` from `mimicry-js`, with `@faker-js/faker` for
realistic values. Name it `camelCase(TypeName) + "Builder"` in a `kebab-case.builder.ts` file, and
migrate test-data-bot or Fishery builders when you touch them.

**Why.** Two builder libraries in one codebase mean two APIs for overrides and traits, and tests copied from
one style break when pasted next to the other.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const makeUser = (overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User => ({ id: "1", name: "Ada", ...overrides });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const userBuilder = build<User>({
  fields: { id: () => faker.string.uuid(), name: () => faker.person.fullName() },
});
```

## Reset builder counters and random state between tests that depend on them

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When a test depends on a generated sequence value or on seeded random output, reset the builder's
counters and seed before each such test. Tests that only use explicit overrides need no reset.

**Why.** Counters and random state live as long as the builder module. A test that expects `id: 1` passes
alone and fails when another test ran first, which shows up as an order-dependent, flaky suite.

## Build structured test data with a builder, not inline object literals

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Take typed test data with three or more fields, nested objects or lists from a builder. Look for an
existing builder first and create one only when none exists; never hand-roll a factory inside a test
or story file. Primitive values and objects with fewer than three fields may stay inline.

**Why.** Hand-written literals copied across tests drift from the type and from each other: adding a required
field breaks every copy, and each test fills the fields it does not care about differently.

## Fill nested typed objects from their own builder

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Give each nested type its own builder and use it as `field: () => otherBuilder.one()`. Override a single
nested key through the parent's `overrides`, which deep-merge, instead of rebuilding the nested object.

**Why.** A nested object written inline in the parent duplicates the child builder's defaults, and the two
drift until the same type looks different depending on which builder made it.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const orderBuilder = build<Order>({
  fields: { customer: { id: "c1", name: "Ada", email: "ada@example.com" } },
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const orderBuilder = build<Order>({ fields: { customer: () => customerBuilder.one() } });
orderBuilder.one({ overrides: { customer: { name: "Ada Lovelace" } } });
```

## Build lists with .many(count), not Array.from or map

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** Build a list of test objects with `builder.many(count, options)`. Pass overrides or traits through its
options instead of mapping over `Array.from` or a spread array.

**Why.** A hand-rolled loop skips the builder's list handling, so overrides and traits have to be repeated per
item and `unique()` values can collide across the list.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const users = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => userBuilder.one({ traits: "admin" }));
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const users = userBuilder.many(3, { traits: "admin" });
```

## Compute fields that derive from other fields in postBuild

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** When a field is computed from other fields of the same object (a total from line items, a full name
from first and last), compute it in the builder's `postBuild`, not in a field generator and not in
each test.

**Why.** A generated derived field ignores overrides of the fields it derives from, so an object built with
custom line items still carries a random total and the test asserts on an impossible object.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
fields: { items: () => itemBuilder.many(2), total: () => faker.number.int() }
```

**Correct:**

```ts
fields: { items: () => itemBuilder.many(2), total: 0 },
postBuild: (order) => ({ ...order, total: order.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0) }),
```

## Call builder.reset() in beforeEach when a test depends on sequence values

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** In a suite whose assertions depend on `sequence()` or `unique()` values, call `.reset()` on the
builder in `beforeEach`. Call `seed(value)` once when the test depends on the output of `oneOf`,
`int`, `float` or `bool`.

**Why.** Counters keep counting across tests in the same module, so `id: 1` is only true for whichever test
runs first.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
test("first order gets id 1", () => {
  expect(orderBuilder.one().id).toBe(1);
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  orderBuilder.reset();
});

test("first order gets id 1", () => {
  expect(orderBuilder.one().id).toBe(1);
});
```

## Use unique() for values that must differ across built objects

_medium · typescript, mimicry-js_

**Rule.** When every built object needs a distinct value from a fixed set (emails, slugs, keys in a list), use
`unique([...])` instead of `oneOf(...)`. Give it at least as many values as the test builds, and reset
the builder between tests that rely on the order.

**Why.** `oneOf()` picks at random, so a `.many()` call can return two objects with the same key, and the test
fails only on the runs where the duplicate happens.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
const tagBuilder = build<Tag>({ fields: { slug: oneOf("news", "blog", "docs") } });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
const tagBuilder = build<Tag>({ fields: { slug: unique(["news", "blog", "docs"]) } });
```
